https://www.jacarandafm.com/news/news/ms.text: Evidence led at the Madlanga Commission of Inquiry shed light on an alleged deal involving sophisticated surveillance equipment. Anastasi Mokgobu/Jacaranda FM News Chief evidence leader Matthew Chaskalson presented WhatsApp messages from the phone of late taxi boss Jothan Msibi, concerning a Czech company that was looking to sell devices known as “catchers”. He explained that the technology can mimic cellphone towers and intercept data from mobile devices. The messages involved Msibi, Katiso “KT” Molefe and suspended Sergeant Fannie Nkosi. A man who identified himself as “Shane”, but was saved in Nkosi’s phone as Shaun Jacobs, contacted the officer about documentation needed for the Czech company to demonstrate its equipment to the South African Police Service. Jacobs sent Nkosi a document and asked him to place it on South African Police Service (SAPS) letterhead or that of an official police unit. Nkosi allegedly signed the document using his force number and a SAPS stamp. The document was then sent to Msibi. Chaskalson told the commission that Msibi subsequently used it in dealings with Molefe and Steve Motsumi as they sought potential buyers for the surveillance equipment in Eswatini. “So, Sergeant Nkosi has represented to the Czech government that the company will be presenting to the SAPS and should be allowed to do so,” said the evidence leader. R1.6 MILLION EQUIPMENT DEAL Chaskalson also presented a flight itinerary showing that Motsumi and Msibi had booked a trip to Europe in connection with the procurement of tactical equipment worth R1.6 million. The equipment was intended for Themy Styles, a company in which Msibi and Molefe were listed as owner and director respectively. “Mr Msibi, Mr Motsumi, Mr Molefe and possibly Sergeant Nkosi were involved in a commercial project which involves the selling of high-tech surveillance systems and jamming technology,” said Chaskalson. ESWATINI DEAL STALLS The proposed sale of the surveillance equipment to Eswatini, however, appears to have stalled. Messages showed Jacobs and Nkosi attempting to finalise a contract between the Czech suppliers and the prospective Swazi buyers. But the process was delayed after Nkosi stopped responding to Jacobs for several weeks. One of Msibi’s messages to Nkosi appeared to express frustration over the delays while also referring to further potential government business. “You know there’s so much work we wanted to do with you. We have many solutions that are in demand by government, but we wanted to do this deal first before we can introduce other solutions,” one of Msibi’s last messages to Nkosi read. Commissioner Advocate Sandile Khumalo questioned Chaskalson about the inference he was drawing from the evidence. Chaskalson suggested the evidence pointed to an alleged fraudulent scheme involving those who were aware of the circumstances surrounding Nkosi’s letter. “The inference is that it’s an out-and-out fraud, but it’s a fraud to which everyone involved in that project is party – everyone involved in that project with knowledge of Sergeant Nkosi’s letter." https://www.westmeathindependent.ie/2026.text: Published: Fri 16 Oct 2026, 6:23 PM MEP Ciaran Mullooly. Just Transition 'failing to create enough jobs in Midlands': MEP Published: Fri 16 Oct 2026, 6:23 PM The level of investment and job creation in the Midlands through the EU Just Transition programme is falling far short of the level required to sustain communities in the region impacted by the loss of peat production, MEP Ciaran Mullooly has warned. A report this week by Indecon found there were issues with "the long-term sustainable impact" of the Just Transition fund. It said projects supported by the EU fund had been expected to create up to 1,094 full or part-time jobs, but that just 183 posts had actually been created. Commenting on this report, MEP Mullooly said he was "disappointed but not surprised" by the findings, which also showed that just €16 million of the €22.2 million allocated to the fund had been drawn down. Government analysis found that more than 1,000 employees and contractors were directly impacted by the transition away from peat production in the Midlands. "This report confirms what I have been saying from day one: announcing proposals and funding is not the same as delivering investment and replacement livelihoods for the people affected," Mr Mullooly said. "The investment and employment our communities were led to expect have not materialised on the scale required. "More alarmingly, I do not believe they will materialise unless the policy changes. The approach is wrong because it is not sufficiently focused on the people and places that lost their livelihoods." Mr Mullooly said the fund should have been built around practical routes into work and stronger support for local employers. "My position has been clear: we needed a skills-based approach, a dedicated apprenticeship scheme and much stronger support for small and medium-sized businesses willing to invest and employ locally. "But the application process was weighed down by red tape, while State aid rules also affected applications." He said the economic consequences of ending peat harvesting and closing power stations in the Midlands reached far beyond the plants themselves. "The ending of peat harvesting by Bord na Móna, the closure of the power stations and the impact on associated businesses struck at the heart of the Midlands economy. "These were political choices with consequences for workers, contractors, families and entire communities. "Peat extraction continues in other European countries, including Latvia and Estonia. People in the Midlands are entitled to ask why their industry was shut down before adequate replacement employment was in place," he added. "People in the Midlands were given barely a year to prepare. A previous government Just Transition Progress Report stated that a transition expected to take ten years had been reduced to twelve months, possibly shorter. "Compare that with Poland, where the agreed coal-mine phase-out timetable runs to the end of 2049 and five regions there have been allocated €3.85 billion from the EU Just Transition Fund for 2021–27. "Our communities deserved the same kind of long-term planning and serious investment," the Independent Ireland representative concluded. https://www.euronews.com/2026/10/26/292-.text: When Oliver Schäfer feels what is on the other end of his line, he quickly realises that this is no ordinary fish. The 34-year-old, from the western German state of North Rhine-Westphalia, is taking part in a predator fishing tournament in the southern Polish city of Rybnik in Poland, together with his Dutch fishing partner Kevin Cremers.On 10 and 11 October, 70 teams with around 150 anglers from all over Europe competed there, according to the German newspaper Bild. Schäfer and Cremers had travelled specifically for the event. As Schäfer told the newspaper, the pair were fishing with a special rod designed for large catfish and a soft plastic lure.Schafer only grasped how enormous his adversary was when the fish broke the surface for the first time. The fight lasted more than 30 minutes. Cremers kept the boat on course against the wind, while Schäfer held.Measured and released againBack on shore, judges measured the catfish at 292 centimetres. It was then returned to the lake, as tournament rules require. Schäfer told Bild that the fish are brought ashore on a tarpaulin so that their protective mucus slime layer is not damaged.However, the catch alone was not enough to win the tournament, which was decided on total points. According to the Berliner Zeitung and the results list of the anglers’ association PZW Katowice published by the Katowice branch of the Polish Angling Association (PZW), the duo finished second with 28,930 points.There are, of course, other impressive specimens in the lake as well. On Instagram, Schäfer reports that he and Cremers targeted zander at sunrise. Their catches, including a fish measuring 81 centimetres, earned them "a good number of points" for the overall standings.Is it the same fish caught last year?The catfish has a backstory. According to media reports, participants believe it is the same fish that was caught during the tournament in October 2025. On that occasion, Polish anglers Krzysztof Pyra and Adrian Gontarz landed a catfish that also measured 292 centimetres. The Berliner Zeitung reports that the fish has not grown any longer since, but has become noticeably more bulkier.International Game Fish Association (IGFA), the sport’s global governing body, keeps catfish records by weight, and there is no official list based on length. According to the German daily Welt Die Welt, Italian angler Alessandro Biancardi landed a catfish measuring 2.85 metres from the River Po in 2023.The Polish city of Rybnik in the Silesian Voivodeship is therefore regarded, especially among anglers, as the place where the longest known catfish has been caught.Schäfer’s dream of a three-metre catfish remains alive even after this angling success. He told BILD he was now "just a hand’s breadth" away.Europe’s largest freshwater fishAccording to Germany’s Federal Agency for Nature Conservation, the European catfish is the continent’s largest native freshwater fish. It can grow up to three metres long and weigh as much as 150 kilograms. Striking features include its scaleless body, broad head and six barbels that help it find its way in murky water.It feeds mainly on fish; larger individuals occasionally prey on small waterbirds or mammals. For 2026, the anglers’ association, the Federal Agency for Nature Conservation and the Ichthyological Society have chosen the catfish as fish of the year.Thriving in warmer watersOriginally, the catfish was native mainly to the Danube and Rhine river systems. Stocking programmes dating back to the 19th century and waterways such as the Main-Danube Canal have since opened up many more habitats to the species, according to the agency.Climate change is also helping. As a warmth-loving species, catfish benefit from rising water temperatures. Biologist Jürgen Geist told the German news magazine Focus that populations are increasing markedly, both in range and in density. By contrast, cold-water species such as the brown trout are among the losers.Warmth also plays a role in Rybnik. The reservoir serves as a cooling basin for a coal-fired power plant, and the heated water is discharged back into it. Because fish feed more actively at higher temperatures, catfish, carp and zander grow faster there, according to Schäfer.Experts say the fish pose little danger to humans. They have only small rasping teeth, and outside the spawning season there is virtually no risk. However, in June 2025, a catfish measuring around two metres in length bit several swimmers in Brombachsee in Middle Franconia, causing minor injuries.
